title: Noninvasive airway devices for the prevention of intra-procedural hypoxemia in obese patients undergoing an upper endoscopy with propofol sedation by a non-anesthesiologist-provider - a randomized controlled trial
summary:
To date, there is no randomized controlled trial demonstrating the benefit of a nasal PAP mask in reducing hypoxemia during endoscopic procedures under sedation administered by non-anesthesiologists. 
In our own retrospective case-control study, we observed a substantial reduction in hypoxemia episodes when the nasal PAP mask was used in overweight individuals undergoing upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, with propofol sedation administered by a non-anesthesiological provider.
conditions: Overweight and obese individuals undergoing upper endoscopy under propofol sedation

interventions.name: Group A: Standard 2 l/min O2 with nasal cannula
Group B: Nasal PAP mask (SuperNO2VA™) with 8 L/min O₂ with valve in the "open" position

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Elective upper endoscopy or a combination of upper and lower endoscopy under sedation
Expected procedure duration < 1 hour
Procedure in left lateral position
BMI 25 – 40 kg/m²
Age ≥ 18 years
ASA I to III without particularly high sedation risk
Administration of propofol mono-sedation by non-anesthesia staff (sedation-trained nurse or physician with experience in intensive care medicine)
SpO₂ > 90% on room air upon arrival at the endoscopy department
Exclusion criteria:
Tracheostoma
BMI <25 or >40 kg/m²
ASA IV or V
ASA III and particularly high sedation risk, requiring the involvement of an anesthesia team
Severe lung disease (at the discretion of the medical team, e.g., need for continuous O₂ supplementation)
Expected procedure duration >1 hour
Pregnancy
Inability to consent
Contraindications to the use of propofol
Additional use of sedatives other than propofol
Diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) and home CPAP therapy
